entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen3968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3969" type="x-p"/> The bond of friendship which Jonathan formed with David was so evidently the main point, that in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">1Sa 18:1</reference> the writer commences with the love of Jonathan to David, and then after that proceeds in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> to observe that Saul took David to himself from that day forward; whereas it is very evident that Saul told David, either at the time of his conversation with him or immediately afterwards, that he was henceforth to remain with him, i.e., in his service. “<hi type="italic">The soul of Jonathan bound itself</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. chained itself; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.44.30">Gen 44:30</reference>) <hi type="italic">to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as his soul</hi>.” The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> ויּאהבו with the suffix ו attached to the imperfect is very rare, and hence the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ויּאהבהוּ (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §249, <hi type="italic">b</hi>., and Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. p. 469). לשׁוּב, to return to his house, viz., to engage in his former occupation as shepherd.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.4">1Sa 18:4</reference> <div eID="gen3970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3971" type="x-p"/> As a sign and pledge of his friendship, Jonathan gave David <hi type="italic">his clothes and his armour</hi>. <hi type="italic">Meil</hi>, the upper coat or cloak. <hi type="italic">Maddim</hi> is probably the <hi type="italic">armour coat</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.39">1Sa 17:39</reference>). This is implied in the word ועד, which is repeated three times, and by which the different arms were attached more closely to מדּיו. For the act itself, compare the exchange of armour made by Glaucus and Diomedes (Hom. <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. vi. 230). This seems to have been a common custom in very ancient times, as we meet with it also among the early Celts (see Macpherson’s <hi type="italic">Ossian</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> <div eID="gen3971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3972" type="x-p"/> And David <hi type="italic">went out</hi>, sc., to battle; <hi type="italic">whithersoever Saul sent him, he acted wisely and prosperously</hi> (ישׂכּיל, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.1.8">Jos 1:8</reference> : see at <reference osisRef="Deut.29.8">Deu 29:8</reference>). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.16">1Sa 18:6-16</reference> <hi type="italic">Saul’s jealousy towards David</hi>.<note placement="foot">The section <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:6-14</reference> is supposed by Thenius and others to have been taken by the compiler from a different source from the previous one, and not to have been written by the same author: (1) because the same thing is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13">1Sa 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:14</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, though in a somewhat altered form, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference> occur again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9-1Sam.19.10">1Sa 19:9-10</reference>, with a few different words, and in a more appropriate connection; (2) because the contents of <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9">1Sa 19:9</reference>, and the word ממּחרת in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.10">1Sa 19:10</reference>, are most directly opposed to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and 1Sa 18:5. On these grounds, no doubt, the lxx have not only omitted the beginning of <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference> from their version, but also <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference>-11. But the supposed discrepancy between <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, - viz., that Saul could not have kept David by his side from attachment to him, or have placed him over his men of war after several prosperous expeditions, as is stated in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, if he had looked upon him with jealous eyes from the very first day, or if his jealousy had broken out on the second day in the way described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference>, - is founded upon two erroneous assumptions; viz., (1) that the facts contained in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:1-5</reference> were contemporaneous with those in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:6-14</reference>; and (2) that everything contained in these two sections is to be regarded as strictly chronological. But the fact recorded in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference>, namely, that Saul took David to himself, and did not allow him to go back to his father’s house any more, occurred unquestionably some time earlier than those mentioned in 1Sa 18:6. with their consequences. Saul took David to himself immediately after the defeat of Goliath, and before the war had been brought to an end. But the celebration of the victory, in which the paean of the women excited jealousy in Saul’s mind, did not take place till the return of the people and of the king at the close of the war. How long the war lasted we do not know; but from the fact that the Israelites pursued the flying Philistines to Gath and Ekron, and then plundered the camp of the Philistines after that (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.52-1Sam.17.53">1Sa 17:52-53</reference>), it certainly follows that some days, if not weeks, must have elapsed between David’s victory over Goliath and the celebration of the triumph, after the expulsion of the Philistines from the land. Thus far the events described in the two sections are arranged in their chronological order; but for all the rest the facts are arranged antithetically, according to their peculiar character, whilst the consequences, which reached further than the facts that gave rise to them, and were to some extent contemporaneous, are appended immediately to the facts themselves. Thus David’s going out whithersoever Saul sent him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>) may indeed have commenced during the pursuit of the flying Philistines; but it reached far beyond this war, and continued even while Saul was looking upon him with jealous eyes. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> contains a general remark, with which the historian brings to a close one side of the relation between David and Saul, which grew out of David’s victory. He then proceeds in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference> to give the other side, and rounds off this paragraph also (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14-1Sam.18.16">1Sa 18:14-16</reference>) with a general remark, the substance of which resembles, in the main, the substance of 1Sa 18:5. At the same time it implies some progress, inasmuch as the delight of the people at the acts performed by David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>) grew into love to David itself. This same progress is also apparent in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13">1Sa 18:13</reference> (“<hi type="italic">Saul made him captain over a thousand</hi>”), as compared with <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> (“<hi type="italic">Saul set him over the men of war</hi>”). Whether the elevation of David into a captain over a thousand was a higher promotion than his appointment over the men of war, or the latter expression is to be taken as simply a more general or indefinite term, denoting his promotion to the rank of commander-in-chief, is a point which can hardly be determined with certainty.</note>  - Saul had no sooner attached the conqueror of Goliath to his court, than he began to be jealous of him. The occasion for his jealousy was the celebration of victory at the close of the war with the Philistines.  <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen3972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3973" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When they came</hi>,” i.e., when the warriors returned with Saul from the war, “<hi type="italic">when</hi> (as is added to explain what follows) <hi type="italic">David returned from the slaughter</hi>,” i.e., from the war in which he had slain Goliath, the women came out of all the towns of Israel, “<hi type="italic">to singing and dancing</hi>,” i.e., to celebrate the victory with singing and choral dancing (see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>), “<hi type="italic">to meet king Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with triangles</hi>.” שׂמהה is used here to signify expressions of joy, a <hi type="italic">fête</hi>, as in Jdg 16:23, etc. The striking position in which the word stands, viz., between two musical instruments, shows that, the word is to be understood here as referring specially to songs of rejoicing, since according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:7</reference> their playing was accompanied with singing. The women who “<hi type="italic">sported</hi>” (משׂחקות), i.e., performed mimic dances, sang in alternate choruses (“<hi type="italic">answered</hi>,” as in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.21">Exo 15:21</reference>), “<hi type="italic">Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands</hi>.”
entries.content_plain:
1Sa 18:6-16 Saul’s jealousy towards David . The section 1Sa 18:6-14 is supposed by Thenius and others to have been taken by the compiler from a different source from the previous one, and not to have been written by the same author: (1) because the same thing is mentioned in 1Sa 18:13 , 1Sa 18:14 , as in 1Sa 18:5 , though in a somewhat altered form, and 1Sa 18:10 , 1Sa 18:11 occur again in 1Sa 19:9-10 , with a few different words, and in a more appropriate connection; (2) because the contents of 1Sa 19:9 , and the word ממּחרת in 1Sa 19:10 , are most directly opposed to 1Sa 18:2 and 1Sa 18:5. On these grounds, no doubt, the lxx have not only omitted the beginning of 1Sa 18:6 from their version, but also 1Sa 18:9 -11. But the supposed discrepancy between 1Sa 18:9 and 1Sa 18:10 and 1Sa 18:2 and 1Sa 18:5 , - viz., that Saul could not have kept David by his side from attachment to him, or have placed him over his men of war after several prosperous expeditions, as is stated in 1Sa 18:2 and 1Sa 18:5 , if he had looked upon him with jealous eyes from the very first day, or if his jealousy had broken out on the second day in the way described in 1Sa 18:10 , 1Sa 18:11 , - is founded upon two erroneous assumptions; viz., (1) that the facts contained in 1Sa 18:1-5 were contemporaneous with those in 1Sa 18:6-14 ; and (2) that everything contained in these two sections is to be regarded as strictly chronological. But the fact recorded in 1Sa 18:2 , namely, that Saul took David to himself, and did not allow him to go back to his father’s house any more, occurred unquestionably some time earlier than those mentioned in 1Sa 18:6. with their consequences. Saul took David to himself immediately after the defeat of Goliath, and before the war had been brought to an end. But the celebration of the victory, in which the paean of the women excited jealousy in Saul’s mind, did not take place till the return of the people and of the king at the close of the war. How long the war lasted we do not know; but from the fact that the Israelites pursued the flying Philistines to Gath and Ekron, and then plundered the camp of the Philistines after that ( 1Sa 17:52-53 ), it certainly follows that some days, if not weeks, must have elapsed between David’s victory over Goliath and the celebration of the triumph, after the expulsion of the Philistines from the land. Thus far the events described in the two sections are arranged in their chronological order; but for all the rest the facts are arranged antithetically, according to their peculiar character, whilst the consequences, which reached further than the facts that gave rise to them, and were to some extent contemporaneous, are appended immediately to the facts themselves. Thus David’s going out whithersoever Saul sent him ( 1Sa 18:5 ) may indeed have commenced during the pursuit of the flying Philistines; but it reached far beyond this war, and continued even while Saul was looking upon him with jealous eyes. 1Sa 18:5 contains a general remark, with which the historian brings to a close one side of the relation between David and Saul, which grew out of David’s victory. He then proceeds in 1Sa 18:6 to give the other side, and rounds off this paragraph also ( 1Sa 18:14-16 ) with a general remark, the substance of which resembles, in the main, the substance of 1Sa 18:5. At the same time it implies some progress, inasmuch as the delight of the people at the acts performed by David ( 1Sa 18:5 ) grew into love to David itself. This same progress is also apparent in 1Sa 18:13 (“ Saul made him captain over a thousand ”), as compared with 1Sa 18:5 (“ Saul set him over the men of war ”). Whether the elevation of David into a captain over a thousand was a higher promotion than his appointment over the men of war, or the latter expression is to be taken as simply a more general or indefinite term, denoting his promotion to the rank of commander-in-chief, is a point which can hardly be determined with certainty. - Saul had no sooner attached the conqueror of Goliath to his court, than he began to be jealous of him. The occasion for his jealousy was the celebration of victory at the close of the war with the Philistines. 1Sa 18:6-7
“ When they came ,” i.e., when the warriors returned with Saul from the war, “ when (as is added to explain what follows) David returned from the slaughter ,” i.e., from the war in which he had slain Goliath, the women came out of all the towns of Israel, “ to singing and dancing ,” i.e., to celebrate the victory with singing and choral dancing (see the remarks on Exo 15:20 ), “ to meet king Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with triangles .” שׂמהה is used here to signify expressions of joy, a fête , as in Jdg 16:23, etc. The striking position in which the word stands, viz., between two musical instruments, shows that, the word is to be understood here as referring specially to songs of rejoicing, since according to 1Sa 18:7 their playing was accompanied with singing. The women who “ sported ” (משׂחקות), i.e., performed mimic dances, sang in alternate choruses (“ answered ,” as in Exo 15:21 ), “ Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands .”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">1Sa 18:18</reference> <div eID="gen3978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3979" type="x-p"/> But David replied with true humility, without suspecting the craftiness of Saul: “<hi type="italic">Who am I, and what is my condition in life, my father’s family in Israel, that I should become son-in-law to the king?</hi>” חיּי מי is a difficult expression, and has been translated in different ways, as the meaning which suggests itself first (viz., “<hi type="italic">what is my life</hi>”) is neither reconcilable with the מי (the interrogative personal pronoun), nor suitable to the context. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 471) and Böttcher give the meaning “<hi type="italic">people</hi>” for חיּים, and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §179, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.) the meaning “<hi type="italic">family</hi>.” But neither of these meanings can be established. חיּים seems evidently to signify the condition in life, the relation in which a person stands to others, and מי is to be explained on the ground that David referred to the persons who formed the class to which he belonged. “<hi type="italic">My father’s family</hi>” includes all his relations. David’s meaning was, that neither on personal grounds, nor on account of his social standing, nor because of his lineage, could he make the slightest pretension to the honour of becoming the son-in-law of the king.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.19">1Sa 18:19</reference> <div eID="gen3979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> But Saul did not keep his promise. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.22">1Sa 18:22</reference> <div eID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3981" type="x-p"/> Saul therefore employed his courtiers to persuade David to accept his offer. In this way we may reconcile in a very simple manner the apparent discrepancy, that Saul is said to have offered his daughter to David himself, and yet he commissioned his servants to talk to David privately of the king’s willingness to give him his daughter. The omission of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.18.21">1Sa 18:21</reference></hi> in the Septuagint is to be explained partly from the fact that בּשׁתּים points back to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.19">1Sa 18:17-19</reference>, which are wanting in this version, and partly also in all probability from the idea entertained by the translators that the statement itself is at variance with 1Sa 18:22. The courtiers were to talk to David בּלּט, “<hi type="italic">in private</hi>,” i.e., as though they were doing it behind the king’s back.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">1Sa 18:23</reference> <div eID="gen3981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3982" type="x-p"/> David replied to the courtiers, “<hi type="italic">Does it seem to you a little thing to become son-in-law to the king, seeing that I am a poor and humble man?</hi>” “<hi type="italic">Poor</hi>,” i.e., utterly unable to offer anything like a suitable dowry to the king. This reply was given by David in perfect sincerity, since he could not possibly suppose that the king would give him his daughter without a considerable marriage portion.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.24-1Sam.18.25">1Sa 18:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen3982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3983" type="x-p"/> When this answer was reported to the king, he sent word through his courtiers what the price was for which he would give him his daughter. He required no dowry (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.34.12">Gen 34:12</reference>), but only a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, i.e., the slaughter of a hundred Philistines, and the proof that this had been done, to avenge himself upon the enemies of the king; whereas, as the writer observes, Saul supposed that he should thus cause David to fall, i.e., bring about his death by the hand of the Philistines.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26-1Sam.18.27">1Sa 18:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen3983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3984" type="x-p"/> But David was satisfied with Saul’s demand, since he had no suspicion of his craftiness, and loved Michal. Even before the days were full, i.e., before the time appointed for the delivery of the dowry and for the marriage had arrived, he rose up with his men, smote two hundred Philistines, and brought their foreskins, which were placed in their full number before the king; whereupon Saul was obliged to give him Michal his daughter to wife. The words “<hi type="italic">and the days were not full</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26">1Sa 18:26</reference>) form a circumstantial clause, which is to be connected with the following sentence, “<hi type="italic">David arose</hi>,” etc. David delivered twice the price demanded. “<hi type="italic">They made them full to the king</hi>,” i.e., they placed them in their full number before him.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.28-1Sam.18.29">1Sa 18:28-29</reference> <div eID="gen3984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3985" type="x-p"/> The knowledge of the fact that David had carried out all his enterprises with success had already filled the melancholy king with fear. But when the failure of this new plan for devoting David to certain death had forced the conviction upon him that Jehovah was with David, and that he was miraculously protected by Him; and when, in addition to this, there was the love of his daughter Michal to David; his fear of David grew into a lifelong enmity. Thus his evil spirit urged him ever forward to greater and greater hardness of heart.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.30">1Sa 18:30</reference> <div eID="gen3985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3986" type="x-p"/> The occasion for the practical manifestation of this enmity was the success of David in all his engagements with the Philistines. As often as the princes of the Philistines went out (sc., to war with Israel), David acted more wisely and prosperously than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was held in great honour. With this general remark the way is prepared for the further history of Saul’s conduct towards David.  <chapter eID="1Sam.18"/> <div eID="gen3986" type="x-p"/>
